item.title: Spanberger fact-checked after Trump mail-voting warning raises military ballot fears
item.description: CNN issued a correction after Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Wolf Blitzer suggested Trump's mail-voting rules could impact military voters abroad.
item.content:encoded:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger claimed the Trump administration was attempting to take away the ability of Americans serving overseas to vote by mail — despite the Postal Service’s final rule explicitly exempting military and overseas ballots from its new requirements.

The Postal Service’s (USPS) final rule at the center of the dispute expressly exempts ballots covered by the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA) from the new federal ballot-mail requirements — though an Obama-appointed federal judge temporarily stayed key provisions of the rule Thursday.

"If you are serving our country abroad, I believe that you should have the ability to cast a vote in our elections. The Trump Administration is attempting to take that ability away," Spanberger wrote on X on Aug. 29.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FROM RESTRICTING MAIL-IN BALLOTS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

The final rule says UOCAVA voters are excluded and explains that the separate treatment reflects the circumstances facing military personnel, their families and other overseas voters.

Spanberger made a similar argument during a CNN interview after anchor Wolf Blitzer raised the possibility that Virginia military personnel overseas could be affected. CNN subsequently returned on air to clarify that UOCAVA ballots are exempt from the new USPS requirements.

"The continued attacks that we're seeing from the Trump administration [are] really just an effort to get people fearful, to get to stay home, and in many cases, to eliminate what is a valid, safe, secure way for people to be able to make their voices heard and to vote," she said.

Blitzer added that Virginia is home to "a lot of military personnel who totally rely on mail-in ballots if they want to be able to express their opinion."

Spanberger agreed, pointing to members of the military and diplomatic services, saying the administration’s actions were impacting them along with other Virginians who find vote-by-mail "a better option."

TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS

Spanberger did not respond to a request for comment, but when reached, a representative for CNN said Blitzer issued an on-air correction Monday.

"On Friday, I interviewed the Democratic governor of Virginia, Abigail Spanberger. We discussed legal challenges to the Trump administration's directives for the Postal Service on mail-in voting," Blitzer said in the correction.

"A comment that may’ve suggested that U.S. military and overseas voters' ballots would be impacted by these directives -- I want to be clear right now, those ballots are exempt from the Postal Service's new rules implementing the president's March executive order. Those groups are covered under [UOCAVA], just to be specific on that point."

An X community note added as an appendix to Spanberger's tweet of her exchange with Blitzer also surfaced the correction.

"Military and overseas voters' UOCAVA ballots are explicitly exempt from the USPS rules implementing the March 2026 executive order; service members abroad can still register/request absentee ballots via the Federal Post Card Application," it read.

Several users also pushed back and cited federal statute as well as the USPS’ own rule.

Others said the governor was allegedly "lying" and suggested she should know of UOCAVA as a former CIA officer.

Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, picked up on her original tweet, responding that he had personally discussed overseas military voting with Trump "many times" and said Trump had consistently made clear he did not want to interfere with Americans serving abroad voting by mail.

"This is completely false," Lee tweeted.

2028 DEM HOPEFUL SLAPS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION WITH LAWSUIT OVER MAIL-IN VOTING AFTER MAJOR SCOTUS VICTORY

The Supreme Court in August handed Trump a largely favorable procedural ruling, staying an earlier injunction after finding that the states’ challenge was premature at that stage.

The ruling did not decide the legality of the administration’s mail-voting policies on the merits. America First Legal President Gene Hamilton previously told Fox News Digital that the court prevented the administration from being effectively "enjoined from thinking" before agencies had settled on concrete policies.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The broader fight over Trump’s mail-voting push remains unresolved.

The Supreme Court stayed a judge's earlier injunction after concluding the administration was likely to prevail on its argument that the challenge was premature, but her latest temporary restraining order sets up yet another speed bump.

item.title: Methodist university denies operating 'hidden' DEI program after undercover video posted of school official
item.description: Undercover video captures a Southern Methodist University staffer describing efforts to keep DEI hidden under a "cultural intelligence" label.
item.content:encoded:
An official at Southern Methodist University was captured on undercover video describing what she called "a lot of maneuvering" surrounding the school’s diversity, equity and inclusion efforts, according to footage released by Accuracy in Media that purports to show how DEI initiatives continued under different names.

The video, shared Monday by school choice activist Corey DeAngelis, alleges SMU renamed its Office of Diversity and Inclusion the Office of Cultural Intelligence as part of an effort to keep DEI programming less visible.

The SMU staff member, who is identified in the video by Accuracy in Media as Danielle Palomo, coordinator for community engagement, social change and intercultural engagement division of student affairs, said, "As you can probably imagine, we've had to do a lot of maneuvering in order to remain kinda hidden under a lot of things. But as long as we can keep doing what we're doing even to a smaller capacity, that is what we're going to do. We're going to do our best."

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY

In the video, an undercover journalist asks Palomo, "I was hoping to see if y'all had any existing, like, equity trainings that maybe y'all provide for staff faculty and that would give us an idea of what to go off of."

Palomo responded, "So, all of that is held through our Office of Cultural Intelligence. As you can probably imagine, we've had to do a lot of maneuvering in order to remain kind of hidden under a lot of things. But my office in particular, we do — we have had trainings like that in the past with students.

TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN ‘MISSES CORE IDEOLOGY' AND MUST TARGET LINGERING DANGER ON CAMPUSES, WATCHDOG WARNS

"It's not going to be as severe, hopefully, as some of the other public universities have had to deal with, but I know that the university is definitely finding its like 'P's and Q's' and it's slowly like working to like rename things and maybe do away with things," Palomo said in the video.

While SMU is a private university, it holds 164 active federal grants totaling nearly $30 million from agencies, including the departments of Defense, Health and Human Services, and Education, according to a May 2025 report by its independent student newspaper, The Daily Campus.

FLORIDA STATE UNIVERSITY HIT WITH FEDERAL CIVIL RIGHTS INVESTIGATION OVER RACE, SEX-BASED SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAMS

The outlet also reported that SMU’s research and development spending has more than tripled since 2010, rising from $18.7 million that year to nearly $59.8 million in fiscal year 2023.

The Trump administration has moved to restrict DEI initiatives at federally funded schools through executive actions and Department of Education directives, though federal judges have blocked portions of those efforts amid constitutional and procedural challenges.

DOJ OPENS PROBE INTO PRESTIGIOUS COLLEGE OVER ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION FAVORING MINORITY STUDENTS

The Department of Education has also warned state education departments they must remove diversity, equity and inclusion policies or potentially lose federal funding.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for SMU said, "SMU does not operate a hidden Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) program. The university does offer activities under the Cultural Intelligence framework that was originally adopted in 2017. Cultural Intelligence focuses on the ability to learn from and understand different perspectives, strengthen relationships and foster mutual respect and community."

"Through this approach, we equip members of our university community with the skills to communicate, lead, teach, coach and innovate effectively across different perspectives and experiences," the spokesperson added. "As with all university programs, SMU regularly reviews its practices to ensure they align with applicable legal requirements and our institutional mission."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, school choice activist Corey DeAngelis said, "The Trump administration should pull every dollar of federal funding from universities that keep pushing DEI after pretending they shut it down. The radical left running these campuses is not rooting out Marxist DEI ideology. They are moving the goalposts, renaming offices and hiding the same agenda under new labels like ‘cultural intelligence.’

CONFIDENCE IN HIGHER EDUCATION SLIPS AFTER BRIEF RECOVERY, GALLUP POLL FINDS

"SMU tuition is $63,736. Parents might be surprised to learn they are paying that much for a Christian university that is still pushing divisive far-left ideology. SMU also takes more than $25 million in federal funding each year. 

"A school charging that kind of tuition does not need taxpayer money to keep DEI alive under another name. If they want to keep the ideology, they can do it without federal funds."

Fox News Digital reached out to Palomo for comment.

item.title: Luke Bryan threatens to 'knock the s--- out of' online trolls trashing his new song
item.description: Luke Bryan told Theo Von he'd confront trolls who accused his "Fish Hunt Golf Drink" song of being AI-generated, calling out teenage critics online.
item.content:encoded:
Luke Bryan has a bone to pick with his haters.

During an appearance on the "This Past Weekend with Theo Von" podcast, the "American Idol" judge and country star opened up about the backlash surrounding his latest song, "Fish Hunt Golf Drink," which some social media users accused of being created with artificial intelligence.

Bryan said the controversy began with a "narrative" created and amplified online.

LUKE BRYAN CREDITS RELIGIOUS ROOTS AND SMALL-TOWN VALUES FOR HELPING HIM NAVIGATE A ‘CHALLENGING LIFE’

"That’s the crazy thing about where we’re at with social [media]," he said. "They started a narrative that we AI-ed it. And now, whether you like the song or not, or whether you like me as an artist, whether you like what I'm about or whatever … now I'm the guy that somebody said that I AI-ed a song and wrote it.

"You get one or two kids with a bunch of Instagram, a bunch of followers, that say we AI-ed it, and then the whole world goes on their narrative."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Von argued that he doesn't think people actually believe he used AI to create the song, but Bryan said the backlash has been "pretty crazy," and he recalled seeing posts from people who told him they hated him.

"And they’re like at a camera going, ‘I hate you.’ … And I’m like, ‘I can see your face. If I see you one day, I’m going to f---ing knock the s--- out of you, dude,’" he said.

However, Bryan acknowledged that many of the online comments were coming from teenagers.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"But then I’m like, ‘Well, wait.’ I’m not sure I’m happy about a bunch of teenagers telling a 50-year-old man he’s a piece of s--- songwriter," he said. "And then I’m like, ‘Dude, you’re 16. You’re talking to a grown man who’s made a s--- ton of money doing this.'

"It’s just so far out there," he added. "I’m like, if I caught my kids doing some stuff like that, I would kill them."

Earlier this year, Bryan addressed the AI accusations shortly after the song's release.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"We’ve had some negativity out there. Some trolls kind of saying that I ‘AI-ed’ it, which is completely false," he told NBC4 at the Memorial Pro-Am on June 3.

"That song was designed for one thing," he added. "To have fun and tell the world what I love to do and what I strive to do."

Songwriters Chase McGill and Matt Dragstrem also shut down the false narrative during an interview with Rolling Stone.

"[Bryan] is the least artificial person I’ve ever met," McGill said. "The only way I’ve actually succeeded in country music, ever, is by sitting in the room with good friends and enjoying making the song up that day. I don’t believe that I would feel any fulfillment from saying, ‘AI, write me a song about whatever.’ That’s not what I signed up for."

The idea behind the song came up organically, said McGill.

"Luke was texting one of his buddies, and the guy was like, ‘Let’s hang soon,’" he said. "Luke sent him an emoji of a fish, an emoji of a deer, an emoji of a golf club and a beer emoji, and said, ‘You pick which one.’ Then he showed it to us. He was like, ‘Dude, this could be a cool song.’

"The dude loves to have fun. He can outfish most people I know. He’s awesome in the woods. I hear he’s really good at golfing," McGill continued. "And the dude can drink pretty well."

item.title: Miami waitress accused of extortion & threatening to send intimate pics after learning she was the other woman
item.description: Nathalie Rodriguez Gonzalez allegedly sent threatening text messages demanding $20,000 after learning the man she was dating had a girlfriend.
item.content:encoded:
Let me start off by saying that I'd never want to discourage anyone from following their heart. There are plenty of success stories out there from people who weren't led astray.

This is not one of those stories. Warning signs surrounded this businessman's decision to pursue a relationship with a waitress he encountered while she was on the job. Chief among those signs was the fact that he was already in a relationship with someone else.

Another contributing factor to the downfall of this short romantic relationship with the waitress is that she didn’t know about his girlfriend.

THIS SHOULD GO WITHOUT SAYING: SENDING YOUR EX'S NUDE TO HER BOSS ISN'T A BIRTHDAY GIFT

When 19-year-old Nathalie Rodriguez Gonzalez found out that she was the side chick, she allegedly sent threatening text messages demanding thousands of dollars from him, reports Local 10.

According to an arrest report from the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office, she sent threatening text messages to the man demanding that he pay up to the tune of $20,000. If he didn’t send it, another $5,000 would be added, and she would send intimate pictures to his girlfriend and his business partner.

Deputies allege that she also said that she would post the images on all of her social media accounts. This started after Rodriguez Gonzalez learned that he had a girlfriend during the "entire time they were together."

DODGERS PITCHER'S WIFE RECEIVES HORRIBLE THREATS DIRECTED AT NEWBORN CHILD

When he refused to pay, she reportedly sent one of the intimate pictures to his business partner. From there she is said to have sent it to the man's girlfriend along with this message, "This will genuinely get posted if he doesn’t wire me money BTW."

The heartbroken waitress, according to deputies, did post a censored version of the image on her TikTok as well as others. There were allegedly more threats made too.

Threats like, "The deportation does not have to happen, but I want my money," and "If he doesn’t wire me the money, his d*** will get posted followed by your face, his face."

Rodriguez Gonzalez was arrested on Friday on charges of threats and extortion. According to deputies, she gave a "full confession."

Again, this shouldn't discourage people from following their hearts. Instead, it should serve as a reminder that sometimes your heart can lead you into choppy romantic waters. Be careful out there.

item.title: Dick Van Dyke shocks fans by posting inversion table workout at age 100
item.description: Dick Van Dyke, 100, shared a video of his inversion table workout on Instagram, proving his lifelong commitment to fitness is still going strong.
item.content:encoded:
When it comes to his fitness, Dick Van Dyke is not slowing down anytime soon.

On Friday, Van Dyke, 100, shared a video of himself stretching on an inversion table.

"#DVD100 1/2 workout inversion table #keepmoving," he captioned the clip, which he shared on Instagram on Friday, Aug. 28.

‘A MAN WITHOUT LOVE’ SINGER ENGELBERT HUMPERDINCK CREDITS UNDERWATER WORKOUT FOR KEEPING HIM ‘ALIVE’ AT 90

Fans took to the comments section to gush about the actor and his athletic skills.

"I love this, let's all work out with DVD! We need you in this world and it makes me happy to see you!" one fan wrote, while another said: "Thank goodness you're doing amazing. Stay healthy."

Other comments from fans include: "He's showing all of us what we could be doing. I'm not of course," "Stretching will definitely help you stay in your best shape," "Truly amazing and inspirational," "This is why you're going to outlive us all and I'm happy to be here for it."

One fan said "Protect this man!!" while another simply wrote: "Very impressive!!!!"

Last year, Van Dyke wrote an essay for The Times U.K., which described how staying active has been key to keeping himself physically strong and mentally sharp.

"I still try to hit the gym three times a week," he explained. "I don’t know why this is something I still want to do, but it is. I’m not a ‘wake up and go back to bed’ type just yet, unless it’s cold and rainy. If I miss too many gym days, I really can feel it — a stiffness creeping in here and there. If I let that set in, well, God help me."

WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS HE'S 'TAKING CARE OF BUSINESS' AT 95: 'THE LEAST OF ALL I WANT DO IS DIE'

"At the gym, I usually do a circuit, going from one machine to the next without a break, in a circle," he said. "I start with the sit-up machine. Arlene says I could do 500, but that might be exaggerating. Then I do all the leg machines religiously, because my legs are two of my most cherished possessions. And then the upper body."

"The secret ingredient is the music," he continued. "Most of my humming and singing really happens when I’m going from one machine to another. By ‘going’ I mean dancing. You heard me — dancing! And if I’m really feeling it, I’m no quiet warbler; I’m a Broadway belter."

ELLEN BURSTYN ON THE HABITS SHE GAVE UP TO STAY THRIVING AT 93 YEARS OLD

Van Dyke also gave up cigarettes and alcohol decades ago.

And when he’s not breaking a sweat, Van Dyke makes it a priority to find something to be grateful for each day.

"He came out of a small Midwestern town," filmmaker Steve Boettcher said. "He wrote a couple of books ago about his hometown, Danville: ‘There’s a rich side of town, and there’s a poor side of town, but there’s not a bad side of town in Danville.’ I think he has a way to see that everything is great in life. He believes there’s always 90% of life that is great and 10% that’s probably not as great — and he’s always focused on that 90%."

item.title: Allies of disgraced ex-House Dem poised for criminal charges for refusing Congress' probe
item.description: Allies of a former House Democrat face DOJ criminal charges after the House unanimously held them in contempt of Congress over defied subpoenas.
item.content:encoded:
Allies of a former House Democrat under federal indictment are now facing potential criminal charges themselves.

The House of Representatives unanimously agreed to hold two people in contempt of Congress on Tuesday — North Miami Beach, Florida, Mayor Michael Joseph and Hector Roos, a former aide to ex-Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, D-Fla. — for failing to work with the House Ethics Committee's investigation into the disgraced Sunshine State Democrat.

It's now up to the Department of Justice (DOJ) whether it pursues criminal charges against both. A contempt of Congress conviction carries a fine of up to $100,000 and up to a year in jail.

DISGRACED DEM CUT OFF FROM DOING BUSINESS WITH GOVERNMENT AFTER ALLEGED ‘OUTRIGHT FRAUD’ UNCOVERED

"The committee cannot fulfill its obligations to safeguard the integrity of the House for witnesses, ignore its subpoenas, and the House cannot accept such willful disregard of its authorities. Mr. Roos and Mr. Joseph willfully fail to comply with multiple subpoenas issued by the committee," Committee Chairman Michael Guest, R-Miss., said.

"They impeded the investigative subcommittee's investigations into the allegations concerning former Representative Cherfilus-McCormick. Those allegations were serious and included violations of federal law to which Mr. Roos and Mr. Joseph were party there. Their conduct warrants referrals to the United States Department of Justice for contempt of Congress."

MIKE JOHNSON SAYS HE SUPPORTS EXPELLING SHEILA CHERFILUS-MCCORMICK OVER DOZENS OF ETHICS VIOLATIONS

The measure passed by voice vote on Tuesday afternoon, meaning lawmakers were not individually put on the record over where they stand. Any lawmaker can stand and object to a voice vote and call for a roll call instead, which none did.

The Democrats present instead signaled they were fully in support of the bid against their fellow left-wingers.

FLORIDA DEM FILED FOR RE-ELECTION DAYS BEFORE RESIGNATION AS HOUSE ETHICS COMMITTEE RAMPED UP PRESSURE

"At a time when public confidence in Congress is at historic lows and the House's ability to self-police member conduct is under intense scrutiny, enforcing lawful congressional process is vital to delivering swift transparency and accountability for any misconduct," Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., said. "A witness who refuses to cooperate with the Ethics Committee hinders the thoroughness and swiftness of an investigation."

Guest charged that Roos "filed inaccurate reports" with the Federal Election Commission while working for Cherfilus-McCormick. He said Roos did not provide adequate justification for not complying with the committee.

"Mr. Joseph was the president of a company that improperly provided corporate funds for the congresswoman's campaign, influenced her staff to submit community funding project requests for entities that he supported," Guest said of the other target.

He said Joseph cited attorney-client privilege in his decision not to comply with the committee, but that lawmakers argued it was not a valid justification to dodge the probe.

INDICTED DEMOCRAT SHEILA CHERFILUS-MCCORMICK REFUSES TO RESIGN AS EXPULSION VOTE LOOMS

Cherfilus-McCormick resigned from Congress earlier this year amid intense pressure from both the left and right. Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., had been threatening to push a resolution to expel her at the time.

The DOJ said she and her co-defendants "conspired to steal" $5 million in emergency federal funds and used the money to bankroll her 2021 congressional campaign.

EXCLUSIVE: WOMAN WHO STOLE $1.7M MEANT FOR HURRICANE VICTIMS GETS PRISON TIME AS DHS CRACKS DOWN ON FEMA FRAUD

"According to the indictment, Cherfilus-McCormick, 46, and her brother Edwin Cherfilus, 51, both of Miramar, worked through their family healthcare company on a FEMA-funded COVID-19 vaccination staffing contract in 2021. In July 2021, the company received an overpayment of $5 million in FEMA funds," the DOJ said in November 2025. "Prosecutors allege that a substantial portion of the misappropriated funds was used as candidate contributions to Cherfilus-McCormick’s 2021 congressional campaign and for the personal benefit of the defendants."

She has pleaded not guilty.
